core: Sound as dialogue, music, effects, ambience, and silence in relation to moving images
Diegetic and nondiegetic sound, sound design, continuity, and sound bridges
An evidence-based method for analyzing how an audio pattern relates to a sequence
supporting: Basic distinctions among sound recording, sound editing, and sound mixing
Foley and ambient sound as parts of a constructed soundscape
J-cuts and L-cuts as sound bridges across image edits
outOfScope: Software tutorials, mixing specifications, production-safety instruction, or licensing advice for music
Analysis or reproduction of copyrighted audio, dialogue, clips, or score excerpts
Claims that a particular sound or silence guarantees one emotion or proves private creative intent

claims.claim: Film sound includes dialogue, music, sound effects, ambient sound, and silence, which can work with moving images to create a designed soundscape.
Sound design spans planned production recording and post-production work, including sound editing and mixing, rather than simply preserving whatever was recorded on set.
Diegetic sound belongs to the story world available to characters, while nondiegetic sound is presented for the audience outside that story world.
Foley and other added details can support the apparent continuity between what viewers see and hear, even when those sounds were constructed after filming.
A sound bridge can overlap audio across a visual cut; a J-cut introduces the next audio before its image and an L-cut lets prior audio continue after the image changes.
Formal viewing can attend to sound effects, noise, music, silence, and diegetic or nondiegetic status alongside visual and narrative evidence.
A defensible sound analysis identifies what is heard, when it begins or ends, whether it belongs to the story world, and how it relates to image before making a qualified interpretation.
